facts.statement: In 1968, Austrian naturalist Georg Ritter von Frauenfeld identified a bird named Aphanapteryx imperialis in paintings by Jacob Hoefnagel from the royal menagerie of Emperor Rudolph II.

facts.statement: The genus name Aphanapteryx means "invisible-wing", derived from the Greek words for unseen and wing.

facts.statement: Due to nomenclatural priority, the genus name Aphanapteryx was later combined with the older specific name bonasia.

facts.statement: Japanese ornithologist Masauji Hachisuka used a 1638 account of yellowish coloration to argue for a distinct species, Kuina mundyi, rather than the red rail.

facts.statement: The red rail is commonly classified in its own genus, Aphanapteryx, but has historically been united with the Rodrigues rail in the genus Erythromachus.
facts.quote: The two are commonly kept as separate genera, Aphanapteryx and Erythromachus, but have also been united as species of Aphanapteryx at times.

facts.statement: Henry Ogg Forbes described the extinct Hawkins's rail as a new species of Aphanapteryx in 1892.
facts.quote: In 1892, the Scottish naturalist Henry Ogg Forbes described Hawkins's rail, an extinct species of rail from the Chatham Islands located east of New Zealand, as a new species of Aphanapteryx; A. hawkinsi.

facts.statement: Gadow proposed that the similarities between the red rail and the Chatham Islands rail resulted from parallel evolution.
facts.quote: Gadow explained the similarity between the two rails as parallel evolution.

facts.statement: Olson suggested in 1977 that the red rail and Rodrigues rail should be kept as separate genera due to considerable divergence despite sharing a common ancestor.
facts.quote: In 1977, Olson stated that though the two species were similar and derived from the same stock, they had also diverged considerably, and should possibly be kept separate.

facts.statement: Cécile Mourer-Chauviré and colleagues classified the red rail and Rodrigues rail as belonging to separate genera in 1999.
facts.quote: The French palaeontologist Cécile Mourer-Chauviré and colleagues also considered the two as belonging to separate genera in 1999.

facts.statement: Cheke and Hume suggested in 2008 that the red rail's loss of feather structure indicated long-term isolation.
facts.quote: According to the British researchers Anthony S. Cheke and Julian P. Hume in 2008, the fact that the red rail lost much of its feather structure indicates it was isolated for a long time.

facts.statement: Julian Hume suggested the ancestors of the red rail may have arrived on the Mascarenes as early as the middle Miocene, though this might be more recent.
facts.quote: He suggested their ancestors could have arrived on the Mascarenes during the middle Miocene at the earliest, but it may have happened more recently.

facts.statement: The red rail was approximately 35 to 40 cm long, with males weighing around 1.3 kg and females around 1 kg.
facts.quote: It was about 35 - 40 cm long, and the male may have weighed 1.3 kg and the female 1 kg.

facts.statement: The red rail had reddish-brown, fluffy, hairlike plumage with a nearly invisible tail and very short wings.
facts.quote: Its plumage was reddish brown all over, and the feathers were fluffy and hairlike; the tail was not visible in the living bird and the short wings likewise also nearly disappeared in the plumage.

facts.statement: The red rail possessed a long, slightly curved brown bill and possibly a nape crest.
facts.quote: It had a long, slightly curved, brown bill, and some illustrations suggest it had a nape crest.

facts.statement: The red rail has been compared to a kiwi and a limpkin in both appearance and behavior.
facts.quote: The bird perhaps resembled a lightly built kiwi, and it has also been likened to a limpkin, both in appearance and behaviour.

facts.statement: The red rail had the largest cranium among Mascarene rails, which was compressed from top to bottom.
facts.quote: The cranium of the red rail was the largest among Mascarene rails, and was compressed from top to bottom in side view.

facts.statement: The red rail's lower jaw rostrum was long, with the mandibular symphysis measuring about 79% of the cranium's length.
facts.quote: The mandibular rostrum of the lower jaw was long, with the length of the mandibular symphysis (where the halves of the mandible connect) being about 79% of the cranium's length.

facts.statement: The red rail's humerus measured 60 to 66 mm with a strongly curved shaft.
facts.quote: The humerus was 60 - 66 mm, and its shaft was strongly curved from top to bottom.

facts.statement: The red rail's femur was very robust, 69 to 71 mm long, with a strongly arched upper shaft.
facts.quote: The femur (thigh-bone) was very robust, 69 - 71 mm long, and the upper part of the shaft was strongly arched.

facts.statement: The red rail's tibiotarsus was large and robust, measuring 98 to 115 mm in length.
facts.quote: The tibiotarsus (lower leg bone) was large and robust, especially the upper and lower ends, and was 98 - 115 mm long.

facts.statement: The red rail's tarsometatarsus was large and robust, measuring 79 mm long.
